title: Arcology: the Laurea, the Fellowship, and the Town on the Mesa
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Turin, the birth in the industrial capital
stops.date_confidence: birth date attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'; Britannica). Coordinate corrected to 45.0792/7.6761, Wikipedia's value for Turin; the pool's 45.0708/7.6858 sits about 1.5 km east, still inside the city.
stops.campa: He is born on the twenty-first of June in Turin, the city that builds Italy's cars. Fiat is headquartered here, and Lancia, and Alfa Romeo; the century's great machine for turning countryside into workforce runs at full speed a few streets from the house. The boy will spend his life on one question, what a city is for, and he begins it inside a city that has already answered: a city is for production. He grows up in the Piedmont under the Alps, in a country that has just finished one war and will shortly start another.
suggested_refs: Turin under the Fiat works, the industrial capital of Piedmont in 1919

stops.name: Politecnico di Torino, the laurea in architecture
stops.date_confidence: the degree year 1946 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'); month and day defaulted. The pool's two lenses disagree about the degree itself, one calling it a laurea, the other a doctorate. The laurea of that era conferred the title dottore in architettura, which is how English sources come to say doctorate; it is not a research doctorate, and the file follows the laurea reading. Coordinate 45.0631/7.6611, Wikipedia's value, about 90 m from the pool's.
stops.campa: He takes his laurea at the Politecnico in the year after the war ends, with Turin bombed and the Italian building trade reduced to rubble clearance. The degree carries the title dottore in architettura, which English-speaking obituaries will later translate as a doctorate; it is the ordinary Italian architectural qualification, and he takes it at twenty-seven. There is no work. There is a continent of ruins and no money to rebuild it with, and a young architect in Piedmont has a choice between waiting and leaving.
suggested_refs: The Politecnico di Torino architecture faculty in the first postwar academic year

stops.name: New York Harbor, the first crossing
stops.date_confidence: December 1946 is attested for the first visit to the United States (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'); the day is defaulted and the port is reconstruction. No source reached names the ship or the point of arrival. New York is the conventional assumption and is pinned as such. GAP declared.
stops.campa: He crosses in December, intending a visit. No manifest reached names his ship or his landing, and the harbour is pinned here because that is where Italians arriving in 1946 arrived. He is twenty-seven, newly qualified, with a language he barely speaks and one name in his head: an old man in Wisconsin who has been telling America for fifty years that its buildings should come out of their own ground. Soleri means to see him. What he intends as a visit lasts, with one long Italian interruption, the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Passenger arrivals at New York from Italian ports, winter 1946

stops.name: Spring Green, Taliesin in the warm season
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri', attests roughly eighteen months in fellowship with Frank Lloyd Wright at Taliesin in Spring Green and at Taliesin West in Arizona; it does not say which months he spent where. The seasonal split follows the Fellowship's documented migration and is reconstruction. Month and day placed at the start of the Wisconsin season. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from frank_lloyd_wright.journey.json, 43.1411/-90.0706; the pool's 43.1462/-90.073 is about 600 m off.
stops.campa: He is taken into the Taliesin Fellowship and comes up the hill above the Wisconsin River, where Frank Lloyd Wright has built and rebuilt a house on the brow rather than the summit because a hill should keep its head. The apprentices farm, cook, quarry stone and draw. Wright is seventy-nine and in a second fame. Soleri learns the doctrine at its source: that a building belongs to its site, its climate and its material, and that the American city as it is currently being built is a disaster with money behind it.
suggested_refs: The Taliesin Fellowship at the Hillside buildings, Spring Green
Wright's Taliesin, 5607 County Road C, Iowa County, Wisconsin

stops.name: Taliesin West, the winter camp under the McDowells
stops.date_confidence: that Soleri's fellowship included Taliesin West is attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'); the specific winter months are reconstruction. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from frank_lloyd_wright.journey.json, 33.6064/-111.8453, which is also Wright's terminal pin after the 1985 relocation of his remains. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The whole school drives to Arizona for the winter: desert masonry of local rock set into concrete forms, redwood trusses, canvas overhead instead of a roof. Soleri has known only the stone cities of Piedmont. Here he meets the Sonoran desert, earth used as a mould, and light treated as a building material. Frank Lloyd Wright bought this ground ten years before and will be brought back to it as ashes in 1985. Soleri will be buried fifty miles north of this camp, on a mesa he has not yet seen.
suggested_refs: Taliesin West, 12621 N. Frank Lloyd Wright Boulevard, Scottsdale, Arizona

stops.name: Museum of Modern Art, the Beast Bridge in print
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Two incompatible accounts sit in the pool. One says a Soleri bridge design gained international notice and was shown at the Museum of Modern Art, dated 1949, with the admission that no firm year appears in the retrieved text. The other says the Beast Bridge was designed for Elizabeth Mock's MoMA book The Architecture of Bridges in 1948. A book and an exhibition are different events, and neither reading was checked against a MoMA record. Both are left standing; the publication reading is pinned. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: A bridge he has drawn goes into a Museum of Modern Art book on the architecture of bridges, and his name reaches print outside Arizona for the first time. Whether the drawing also hung on a MoMA wall is a thing the sources say differently and this atlas does not settle. The design is a span shaped like an animal, structure and creature at once, and it sets the habit of a lifetime: he thinks in single continuous objects rather than assemblies of parts. Sixty-two years later, the last work he completes will also be a bridge.
suggested_refs: Elizabeth Mock, The Architecture of Bridges, Museum of Modern Art, 1949
sources: secondary biographical summary citing the MoMA publication record

stops.name: Camelback Mountain, the camp after the Fellowship
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout. Sources give 1947 or 1948 for the departure from Taliesin and disagree on whether Wright dismissed the pair or they left of their own will; Wikipedia's 'Mark Mills (architect)' says 1948, which is used here. The figure of roughly 240 days camping has no attributable source and is carried as an unsourced round number. Place corrected: Camelback Mountain is in Phoenix, between the Arcadia neighbourhood and the town of Paradise Valley, not in Scottsdale. Coordinate corrected to 33.5147/-111.9616, about 700 m from the pool's. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He leaves the Fellowship with a fellow apprentice, Mark Mills, and the two camp on the red hump of rock between Phoenix and Paradise Valley while they wait for work. Whether Wright threw them out or they walked is a question the sources answer both ways. Accounts put the camp near two hundred and forty days, a number no document supports. A trained architect with no commissions spends the better part of a year sleeping on a mountain inside the city he will argue against for the next fifty.
suggested_refs: Camelback Mountain between Arcadia and Paradise Valley, Phoenix
sources: secondary biographical summary, contradictory on year and circumstance

stops.name: Cave Creek, the Dome House built into the ground
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's 'List of historic properties in Cave Creek, Arizona' states the Dome was built in 1949, at 7199 E. Grapevine Road, NRHP reference #100002208, listed 15 March 2018; the pool's span of 1948-1950 is narrowed accordingly. The client's name is contradicted between sources, Nora Wood in Wikipedia's 'Mark Mills (architect)' against Lenora or Leonora Woods elsewhere, and is not resolved here. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Their first commission after Taliesin: a house at 7199 East Grapevine Road with a glass dome that turns on a track, set down into the desert floor so that the earth does the cooling. Soleri and Mills build it themselves. The client is named Nora Wood in one source and Lenora Woods in others, and this atlas does not choose between them. Her daughter Carolyn, called Colly, is on the site. He marries her. Sixty-nine years after the house goes up, the United States puts it on the National Register.
suggested_refs: The Dome House, 7199 E. Grapevine Road, Cave Creek, NRHP reference #100002208
sources: Wikipedia, 'List of historic properties in Cave Creek, Arizona'

stops.name: Genoa, the crossing back to Italy
stops.date_confidence: the 1950 return to Italy with Colly is attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'); the port is reconstruction, no source reached naming it. Genoa is pinned as Italy's principal transatlantic port of the period. Month and day defaulted. GAP declared.
stops.campa: He goes home married. No source names the port and this pin is a reasonable guess rather than a record: Genoa is where the liners came in. He has an American wife, one built house behind him and no reputation in his own country. Italy in 1950 is rebuilding at speed on public money and cheap concrete, and for five years he works inside that boom instead of against it. It is the only stretch of his life in which he is an ordinary practising architect taking ordinary commissions.
suggested_refs: The transatlantic passenger terminal at Genoa in the reconstruction years
sources: reconstruction: no source names the port of return

stops.name: Vietri sul Mare, the Solimene ceramics factory
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's 'Vietri sul Mare' states that the Palazzo Solimene was built after the Second World War by Paolo Soleri; the commission is generally dated to the mid-1950s and 1955 is the pool's year. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 40.7259/14.7286 lies about 6 km inland toward Cava de' Tirreni, off the Amalfi coast entirely. 40.674/14.728 is approximate to the building rather than surveyed.
stops.campa: On the Amalfi coast he builds a ceramics factory faced in the pots it makes: rows of terracotta vessel bottoms set into the curving front wall, so that the product becomes the skin. The plan spirals, and the workers move up through it with the material. It is his one substantial European building and the first proof that his drawings stand up in fired clay and concrete. Half a century later the coast boats are still shown the wall of pots, and it is the only work of his that most Italians will ever see.
suggested_refs: Ceramica Artistica Solimene, Palazzo Solimene, Vietri sul Mare

stops.name: Paradise Valley, the five acres bought
stops.date_confidence: the 1956 land purchase in Paradise Valley is attested (Wikipedia, 'Cosanti'; Wikipedia, 'Arcosanti'). The pool's chronology lens said the family settled in Scottsdale; Paradise Valley is a separately incorporated town adjacent to it and the site is in Paradise Valley. The elder daughter's name, given as Kristine in the pool, does not appear in the retrieved Wikipedia text and is not used. Coordinate 33.56683/-111.94191, Wikipedia's value for Cosanti; the pool's geography lens carried 33.5688/-111.9508 at four entries, all corrected. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Paolo and Colly come back from Italy for good, with their elder daughter, and buy five acres of desert a few miles from Taliesin West. The land is dust and creosote. He begins building the way he learned at Cave Creek and will teach for the next half century: pile up a mound of earth, carve the pattern into its surface, pour concrete over the mound, then dig the earth out from underneath. The desert is both the formwork and the quarry. Nothing standing here was fully drawn before it was dug.
suggested_refs: Cosanti, 6433 E. Doubletree Ranch Road, Paradise Valley, Arizona

stops.name: Cosanti, official activities begin
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's 'Arcosanti' states that official activities began at Cosanti in 1959. The pool's chronology lens claimed no discrete founding date existed and tagged the site as reconstruction; two discrete dates do exist, 1956 for the land and 1959 for the activities, and the entry is retagged as attested. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The compound becomes an institution: studios, apses open to the south, a foundry. He casts bronze wind bells and fires ceramic ones, sells them, and pays for the architecture with them. Apprentices arrive to learn earth-casting and stay to make bells. The economic model of his whole working life is set in this yard. The buildings are not paid for by clients. They are paid for by objects made on site and sold to the visitors who came to look at the buildings.
suggested_refs: The Cosanti bronze foundry and the Soleri wind bells

stops.name: Museum of Modern Art, the Mesa City drawings
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The claim that Mesa City drawings entered the Museum of Modern Art's Architecture and Design collection in 1960 comes from a secondary biographical summary citing Scottsdale Museum of Contemporary Art exhibition materials; no MoMA accession record was reached. The study itself is dated 1958-1967 in the same summary. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Mesa City is a drawing rather than a place: a city for two million people laid out across a desert tableland, worked at for nine years, with a university at its centre and no cars in it. The sheets are enormous, inked at a scale that makes the eye walk. New York takes some of them, on the word of a later exhibition catalogue rather than of any accession record this atlas reached. He is designing cities that will not be built and lodging the drawings where built cities go to be looked at.
suggested_refs: The Mesa City scroll drawings, 1958-1967
sources: secondary biographical summary citing SMoCA exhibition materials

stops.name: Tempe, the lectures at Arizona State
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri', attests that he lectured in the College of Architecture at Arizona State University; no source reached gives a start year, an end year or a rank. The date 1962-01-01 is a placement in mid-career and is not a fact. GAP declared. Coordinate corrected to 33.4209/-111.934, Wikipedia's value for the Tempe campus, about 600 m from the pool's.
stops.campa: He teaches in the College of Architecture at Arizona State, across the valley from his own yard. No record reached says when he started or when he stopped. Students come out of the lecture room and drive to Paradise Valley to shovel earth. The arrangement holds for years: a man with almost no built work, arguing from a mound of dirt that the American way of settling land is a slow catastrophe, is given a room in a state university to say it in, at the centre of the fastest-sprawling metropolitan area in the country.
suggested_refs: The College of Architecture, Arizona State University, Tempe

stops.name: Cosanti, the gold medal and the fellowship
stops.date_confidence: the American Institute of Architects Gold Medal for Craftsmanship in 1963 and the Guggenheim Fellowship in Architecture, Planning and Design in 1964 are both attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'). Neither has an attested ceremony location, so both are pinned at Cosanti and the stop is dated at the earlier of the two years. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The American Institute of Architects gives him its Gold Medal for Craftsmanship, and the year after, the Guggenheim Foundation gives him a fellowship in architecture, planning and design. The profession has decided what he is: a maker of beautiful things, a craftsman. He has built one factory in Italy, one house at Cave Creek and a compound of his own. Everything else is drawings and bells. He accepts the medal and goes on digging holes in the ground and pouring concrete into them.
suggested_refs: AIA Gold Medal for Craftsmanship, 1963
Guggenheim Fellowship in Architecture, Planning and Design, 1964

stops.name: Santa Fe, the amphitheater on the Cerrillos Road campus
stops.date_confidence: the 1966 start of design work is attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'). Venue corrected: Wikipedia's 'Paolo Soleri Amphitheater' places it on the campus of the Institute of American Indian Arts at 1501 Cerrillos Road, a campus now occupied by the Santa Fe Indian School, so the pool's naming of the Indian School in 1966 is anachronistic. It opened in 1970, closed in 2010, was marked for demolition in 2011 and was still standing as of 2022. Coordinate 35.6724/-105.9678, a site the pool's geography lens omitted. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He designs an open-air theatre for the Institute of American Indian Arts in New Mexico, earth-cast, sunk into the ground, its stage facing the mountains. It opens in 1970 and becomes for forty years the place where Native performance in the Southwest is staged. In 2010 it is closed, in 2011 it is marked for demolition, and in 2022 it is still standing, neither used nor knocked down. It is the only major public building he completes outside Arizona, and the only one whose fate is settled by an institution that is not his.
suggested_refs: The Paolo Soleri Amphitheater, 1501 Cerrillos Road, Santa Fe

stops.name: Cambridge, Arcology published by the MIT Press
stops.date_confidence: first publication in 1969 with the MIT Press is confirmed by Open Library and by the standard bibliographic record, and Wikipedia's 'Arcology' independently dates the coinage of the word to 1969. A Britannica summary consulted in the research pass instead associated Soleri with this title in 2006, apparently conflating it with his 2006 Cooper Hewitt award year; the discrepancy is recorded and not resolved. Month and day defaulted. Cambridge pinned on the canonical atlas coordinate 42.3601/-71.0942.
stops.campa: The book is called Arcology: The City in the Image of Man, and the word in the title is his own, architecture and ecology pressed together. The argument runs: spread a city out and it eats land, fuel and time, so fold it up instead, one continuous structure, dense, walkable, three-dimensional, with the desert left alone around it. Buckminster Fuller has been making a related case from a different shape since the geodesic domes of 1948. The plates show arcologies for millions. Not one of them is under construction.
suggested_refs: Paolo Soleri, Arcology: The City in the Image of Man, MIT Press, 1969
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Paolo Soleri' (dating the title to 2006, a discrepancy left open)

stops.name: Corcoran Gallery of Art, the retrospective opens
stops.date_confidence: the Corcoran organized the show, and the Whitney's exhibition archive names it The Architectural Vision of Paolo Soleri; the pool's chronology lens called it City in the Image of Man, which is the title of the book and not of the exhibition. The Washington run of 20 February to 5 April 1970 comes from a secondary catalogue summary and could not be independently confirmed, so the days are provisional. Coordinate corrected to 38.8958/-77.0399, 500 17th Street NW, about 230 m from the pool's.
stops.campa: Washington gives him a full retrospective: the models, the enormous scroll drawings, the arcology schemes named like species. Crowds come. The show is called The Architectural Vision of Paolo Soleri and the book on sale at the door is called City in the Image of Man, a pairing that later summaries will confuse into a single title. He is fifty and has never built a city, or a quarter of one, or a street. What the visitors are looking at exists almost entirely as ink on paper and plaster on tables.
suggested_refs: The Architectural Vision of Paolo Soleri, Corcoran Gallery of Art, spring 1970
sources: secondary catalogue summary for the Washington dates

stops.name: Whitney Museum of American Art, the New York leg
stops.date_confidence: the Whitney's own exhibition archive records The Architectural Vision of Paolo Soleri as running 17 July to 20 September 1970, organized by the curator James Monte. The pool dated the opening 20 September, which is the closing date; the inversion would have moved the stop two months. Coordinate 40.7735/-73.9631, the Breuer building at 945 Madison Avenue, occupied 1966-2014.
stops.campa: The show travels to Madison Avenue and runs through the summer inside Marcel Breuer's inverted granite ziggurat, hung by the curator James Monte. It closes on the twentieth of September, after two months on the wall. New York in 1970 is the densest city in the country. It is already an arcology of a sort, and it is also the machine the drawings are meant to replace. That autumn, four hundred miles of desert away, ground is broken on the only arcology he will ever start.
suggested_refs: The Whitney at 945 Madison Avenue, Breuer building, exhibition of 17 July to 20 September 1970

stops.name: Cordes Junction, ground broken at Arcosanti
stops.date_confidence: construction beginning in 1970 on land near Cordes Junction is attested (Wikipedia, 'Arcosanti'; Britannica). Month and day are defaulted to 01, which places the stop's nominal date before the two 1970 exhibition stops; the ordering in this file follows the events as narrated rather than the defaulted date.
stops.campa: Seventy miles north of Phoenix, on a mesa above the Agua Fria, he begins an experimental town for five thousand people, to be built by the people who come to live in it. Students pay tuition to pour its concrete. The apses face south so that the low winter sun enters and the high summer sun does not. Tommaso Campanella wrote his city of the sun in a Neapolitan prison and never saw a stone of it laid; Soleri has a cement mixer, a hillside and volunteers who pay for the privilege of being there.
suggested_refs: Arcosanti on the mesa above the Agua Fria, Yavapai County, Arizona

stops.name: Garden City, the bridge between matter and spirit
stops.date_confidence: the 1973 publication is attested (Britannica); the place is corrected. The full title is The Bridge Between Matter & Spirit is Matter Becoming Spirit: The Arcology of Paolo Soleri, published by Anchor Books, Garden City, New York, per the citation in Wikipedia's 'Arcology' and the Internet Archive catalogue; the pool placed it at Arcosanti or Cosanti in Arizona. The coordinate is approximate to Garden City and was not surveyed. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The second book comes out of a New York suburb rather than out of the desert: Anchor Books, Garden City, under a title that is a whole sentence, The Bridge Between Matter and Spirit is Matter Becoming Spirit. The arcology is no longer only an engineering proposal. It is now a stage in the evolution of consciousness, the planet complexifying, matter thinning out into mind. He is building a town with students and hand-mixed concrete and describing it in the language of a cosmology.
suggested_refs: Anchor Books edition, Garden City, New York, 1973

stops.name: Arcosanti, the redesign for the sun
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's 'Arcosanti' dates a major redesign incorporating alternative energy sources to 1975-1977; the stop is pinned at the start of that span. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Five years in, with the oil embargo behind everyone, the plan is opened up and redrawn to take its energy from the sun. Greenhouses are set below the residential terraces so that the heat they trap in winter rises into the buildings above them. He calls the principle the two suns: one sun for light, one for the work the light does. The town on the ground is still a few vaults, a foundry and a hillside of rebar, and the plan for it has by now been revised more times than the site has buildings.
suggested_refs: The 1975-1977 Arcosanti redesign and the greenhouse terraces

stops.name: Rochester, the Two Suns Arcology exhibition
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri', places the Two Suns Arcology exhibition at the Xerox Square Center, Rochester, New York, in 1976; the pool's chronology lens gave only 'United States'. Coordinate approximately 43.1566/-77.6088. Wikipedia's 'Arcosanti' ties the two-suns concept to the 1975-1977 redesign, so the exhibition and the redesign are one argument in two places. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The revised argument goes on show in a corporate plaza in upstate New York, in the lobby of a photocopier company's tower. Models of solar arcologies stand inside a sealed glass box conditioned by machinery, and the audience is office workers passing through. He is showing the alternative inside the thing he objects to. The drawings tour, the crowds come, and the only construction site is a mesa in Yavapai County staffed by students who pay tuition to work on it.
suggested_refs: Two Suns Arcology, Xerox Square Center, Rochester, New York, 1976

stops.name: Vancouver, the first Habitat conference
stops.date_confidence: Soleri's participation in the United Nations' first Habitat conference on human settlements at Vancouver in 1976 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'). The conference ran in late May and early June 1976; the day is defaulted and the month is a placement rather than a pool-attested fact. Canonical Vancouver coordinate 49.2827/-123.1207.
stops.campa: The United Nations convenes its first conference on human settlements and he is one of the voices in the hall. The subject is the thing he has been drawing since Mesa City: how the species is to house four billion people, and then twice that, without paving the arable surface of the earth. Governments are there, and squatters' movements, and architects. For a fortnight his position is not eccentric but on the agenda of the world, argued in a coastal city that is spreading up its own valleys as fast as it can.
suggested_refs: UN Habitat I, Vancouver, 31 May to 11 June 1976

stops.name: Arcosanti, the year Newsweek came
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri', attests the 1976 Newsweek feature on Arcosanti; no source reached gives the issue or the month, and month and day are defaulted. The quotation was seen only as it appears on Wikipedia at footnote 9; the original 1976 article was not reached and the wording is therefore mediated.
stops.campa: A national magazine comes out to the mesa and calls what is happening there the most important urban experiment of the age. Visitors begin arriving by the thousand. The workshops fill; young people pay to spend a summer mixing concrete for a town meant to hold five thousand and holding perhaps fifty. The sentence is still quoted fifty years on. No source reached gives the issue or the month, and the wording comes down through later writers rather than from the magazine itself.
stops.quote: the most important urban experiment undertaken in our time
stops.quote_source: Newsweek, 1976, on Arcosanti, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri' (footnote 9); the original article was not reached
suggested_refs: Newsweek's 1976 feature on Arcosanti

stops.name: Arcosanti, the phase called Critical Mass
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's 'Arcosanti' attests the introduction of Critical Mass as a developmental phase for the project in 1980; the source does not define the threshold in numbers, and no population figure is asserted here. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He names the next phase Critical Mass: the population and the built fabric the town has to reach before it starts working as a town rather than as a construction site. The sources do not record what number he set. Ten years of volunteers have produced a foundry, a ceramics apse, vaults, an amphitheatre and housing for a few dozen. The phase is announced. It is never entered. The word critical keeps its physics meaning here, the threshold below which a reaction does not sustain itself.
suggested_refs: The Critical Mass phase of the Arcosanti development plan, 1980

stops.name: Sofia, the gold medal of the World Biennale
stops.date_confidence: the Gold Medal at the World Biennale of Architecture in Sofia in 1981 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'); month and day defaulted. Canonical Sofia coordinate 42.6977/23.3219.
stops.campa: Bulgaria gives him the gold medal of its architecture biennale, on the far side of a border that in 1981 is closed to most of the profession's traffic. The socialist bloc has been building dense planned settlements at scale for thirty years and reads his drawings as an argument it already accepts. In Arizona the same drawings read as counterculture. The medal joins the others in the desert compound, and the town on the mesa goes on being built at the rate volunteers build.
suggested_refs: The World Biennale of Architecture, Sofia, 1981

stops.name: Phoenix, the DeConcini House
stops.date_confidence: the 1982 DeConcini House in Phoenix is attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'; Britannica); no source reached gives a street address, so the pin is central Phoenix and is a placement rather than a location. Month and day defaulted. GAP declared.
stops.campa: A private house in Phoenix, for the DeConcini family. It is a rarity by this point: an ordinary commission, from a client, for a single dwelling, of the sort an architect his age would normally have built two hundred of. He has instead spent thirty years arguing that the single dwelling on its own lot is the problem itself. The house is his, and the city it stands in has by now spread across an area of desert larger than some countries, one lot at a time.
suggested_refs: The DeConcini House, Phoenix, 1982; street address not established

stops.name: Cosanti, the death of Colly Soleri
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source reached gives a date for Carolyn Woods Soleri's death from cancer; Wikipedia places it four years before the 1986 Cancer Center Chapel commission, which yields about 1982 by subtraction. That is arithmetic on a source's adverb rather than a date. The place is inferred too, nothing reached saying where she died. Month and day defaulted. GAP declared.
stops.campa: Colly dies of cancer. No document reached gives the day, or the month, or the place; the year is worked backwards from a sentence saying she died four years before a commission he took in 1986. She had been with him since the Cave Creek site, through Vietri, through the five acres and the bells and the mesa, thirty-two years. This atlas can date the founding of a bell foundry to the year and cannot date this. She is buried at Arcosanti, and he will be laid beside her thirty-one years later.
suggested_refs: The Arcosanti cemetery, burial place of Carolyn Woods Soleri
sources: Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri' (dating her death only relative to the 1986 commission)

stops.name: Cosanti Press, the urban laboratory question
stops.date_confidence: the year is disputed and is not resolved here. Wikipedia and Britannica give 1983; Open Library records the first edition of Arcosanti: An Urban Laboratory? as 1984, from VTI Press, Cosanti Press and Avant Books, with a second edition from Cosanti Press in 1993. The stop is dated 1983 and both records are carried. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: He publishes an account of the town under a title that ends in a question mark: Arcosanti, an urban laboratory? Thirteen years of construction stand behind it. The catalogues disagree about whether the first edition is 1983 or 1984, and this atlas leaves them disagreeing. The question in the title is not rhetorical. A laboratory produces results legible to people who were not present, and what the mesa has produced so far is a partial town, a bell foundry and a very large number of visitors.
suggested_refs: Paolo Soleri, Arcosanti: An Urban Laboratory?, first edition 1983 or 1984

stops.name: Paris, the silver medal of the Academie d'Architecture
stops.date_confidence: the Silver Medal of the Academie d'Architecture in 1984 is attested (Wikipedia, 'Paolo Soleri'); month and day defaulted. Pinned on the canonical atlas Paris coordinate 48.8566/2.3522, which the interlock lens instructs this file to inherit rather than mint a new one.
